parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the work function energy of a metal.

markscheme_points.text: minimum energy to remove electron or energy to remove electron from surface or energy to remove electron with zero kinetic energy

hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds an electron inside a metal and what light must supply for the electron to escape completely.
Hint 2: Focus on the word minimum - consider an electron just at the surface that leaves with no spare kinetic energy.
parts.proper_answer: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the metal, so that it leaves with zero kinetic energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture An Electron Trapped In The Metal**
Electrons in a metal need extra energy to break free from the attraction of the positive ions. Light supplies this energy in packets called photons, with one photon giving all its energy to one electron.

Step 2: **Why Minimum And Surface Matter**
Electrons deeper inside lose extra energy in collisions on the way out. The easiest escape is for an electron right at the surface that just barely gets free. That smallest needed energy is called the work function energy $\Phi$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Ultraviolet radiation of frequency $1.36 \times 10^{15} \text{Hz}$ is incident, in a vacuum, on a metal surface. The power of the radiation incident on the surface is $8.36 \text{mW}$. Photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy of $3.09 \times 10^{-19} \text{J}$.
parts.text: Determine the number of photons incident on the surface per unit time.
hints: Hint 1: Start from what power means - total light energy arriving per second - and think how that total is shared among many identical photons.
Hint 2: Recall how the energy of a single photon is linked to frequency, then divide the total power by that single-photon energy.
parts.proper_answer: Number per unit time $= P/hf = 9.27 \times 10^{15} \text{ s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Of One Photon**
Each photon carries energy determined by frequency: $$E = hf$$ With $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $f = 1.36 \times 10^{15} \text{ Hz}$: $$E = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 1.36 \times 10^{15} \approx 9.02 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Divide Total Power By One Photon**
Power is energy per second. Convert $8.36 \text{ mW} = 8.36 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W}$. If $N$ is photons per second: $$P = N hf$$ $$N = \frac{P}{hf} = \frac{8.36 \times 10^{-3}}{9.02 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 9.27 \times 10^{15} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the work function energy $\Phi$ of the metal.
hints: Hint 1: Think of energy book-keeping for one electron - the photon energy is split into the cost of escape plus what is left as kinetic energy.
Hint 2: Identify which kinetic energy gives the work function - the maximum value, for a surface electron - then rearrange to find $\Phi$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Einstein's Photoelectric Equation**
For the fastest electrons, no extra energy is lost inside: $$hf = \Phi + E_{max}$$ Here $hf$ is already known to be about $9.02 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ and $E_{max} = 3.09 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$.

Step 2: **Solve For The Work Function**
Rearrange before substituting: $$\Phi = hf - E_{max}$$ $$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 1.36 \times 10^{15}) - 3.09 \times 10^{-19}$$ $$\Phi \approx 9.02 \times 10^{-19} - 3.09 \times 10^{-19} = 5.93 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The frequency of the radiation incident on the surface in (b) is increased while the power remains constant.

State and explain the effect of this change on:
parts.text: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons

markscheme_points.text: greater photon energy (and same work function)
so maximum kinetic energy is increased

hints: Hint 1: Consider what happens to the energy carried by each individual photon when frequency is raised.
Hint 2: Remember the metal itself is unchanged, so think how the extra photon energy must appear after the fixed escape cost is paid.
parts.proper_answer: Maximum kinetic energy increases because photon energy $hf$ is greater while $\Phi$ is unchanged, so $E_{max} = hf - \Phi$ increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Greater Frequency Means Greater Photon Energy**
Since $E = hf$, increasing $f$ gives each photon more energy. The metal is the same, so its work function $\Phi$ stays constant.

Step 2: **More Leftover Energy As Kinetic Energy**
From $E_{max} = hf - \Phi$, a larger $hf$ minus the same $\Phi$ leaves a larger remainder. So the fastest photoelectrons emerge with greater maximum kinetic energy.

key_concepts: fixed work function for same metal

Hint 2: Remember the metal itself is unchanged, so think how the extra photon energy must appear after the fixed escape cost is paid.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the rate of emission of photoelectrons.

markscheme_points.text: (greater photon energy and same power so) lower number of photons (per unit time)
(each electron absorbs one photon) so lower rate of emission

hints: Hint 1: Think about keeping total power fixed while each photon becomes more energetic - what must happen to the count of photons arriving each second?
Hint 2: Link photons to electrons on a one-to-one basis and decide what fewer photons per second means for emitted electrons per second.
parts.proper_answer: Rate of emission decreases because at constant power, larger $hf$ means fewer photons per unit time, and each photon releases at most one electron.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Same Power But Bigger Packets**
Power is $P = N hf$. If $P$ is constant and $hf$ increases, $N$ must fall: $$N = \frac{P}{hf}$$ So fewer photons strike the surface each second.

Step 2: **Fewer Photons Means Fewer Electrons**
In the photoelectric effect one photon is absorbed by one electron. With fewer photons per second available, fewer electrons can be released per second, so the photoelectric current or rate of emission decreases even though each electron is faster.
